c.text: Chapter 4 – Building a Volunteer Team
Why a general announcement may not be enough
Every new leader tries it once.
You stand up, describe the need, say the ministry is desperate for help, and ask anyone who feels led to see you afterwards.
Sometimes nobody responds.
Sometimes someone responds whose gifts or availability do not match the role you had in mind.

A general appeal can leave people unsure whether the role suits them or what it involves. A clear invitation helps. Keep an open, fair route for people to express interest, then use the same role criteria and checks for everyone. Personal invitations can complement that process without turning recruitment into a circle of favourites.
The biblical examples that follow show leaders making deliberate choices about who would carry responsibility.
Moses was drowning until his father-in-law fixed it

Exodus 18:13-26 is the most practical management passage in the Bible. Jethro, Moses’ father-in- law, visits the camp and watches Moses sit as judge from morning until evening while the people stand around him waiting.
His assessment in verse 17 is blunt: what you are doing is not good. He tells Moses he will wear himself out, and the people with him, because the work is too heavy to carry alone.
Then he gives the solution in verses 21 and 22.

Select capable men from all the people – men who fear God, who are trustworthy, and who hate dishonest gain – and appoint them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them judge the ordinary cases and bring only the difficult ones to Moses.
Three things are worth pulling out.
The criteria are character, not availability. Capable, God-fearing, trustworthy, not greedy. Not “willing” and not “free on Thursdays.”
They are selected, not volunteered.
Moses goes and chooses.
They are given real decisions.
Jethro does not suggest Moses keep all the authority and hand out the chores. He tells him to let them judge. A team that cannot decide anything is not a team – it is a set of errands.
Jesus prayed all night, then picked twelve
Luke 6:12-13 says Jesus went out to a mountainside and spent the night praying to God, and when morning came he called his disciples to him and chose twelve of them.
An entire night of prayer before choosing a team.
Most of us choose in the corridor after a service.
Mark 3:13-14 adds the purpose.

He appointed twelve that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach. Being with him comes first – the relationship before the deployment. He did not recruit twelve functionaries to cover the workload; he built people, and the work came out of that.
There is a warning buried in this for us.
If your only contact with your volunteers is about their tasks, you have a rota, not a team. Chapter 5 is about the difference.
Who to ask
Look for four things, roughly in this order.
Character.
Acts 6:3 set the bar at people of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom – and that was for handling food distribution. If the early church demanded that for a practical task, so can you.
Faithfulness in something small already.

In 2 Timothy 2:2, Paul tells Timothy to entrust teaching to faithful people able to teach others. Look for evidence of reliability, but ask about context. Doing one task well does not prove readiness for every role; leaving a previous ministry does not prove unfaithfulness.
Some evidence of the gift.

1 Corinthians 12 is Paul’s long argument to a divided Corinthian church that the body has many parts with different functions, and that the parts that seem weaker are indispensable. Practically: match people to what they are actually good at rather than to your empty slots. A gifted administrator forced to lead worship will fail at both.
Teachability over talent.
You can train a humble person with average ability. You cannot train someone who already knows.
One more note.
Do not recruit only people like yourself. It is the natural instinct and it produces a team with one set of strengths and one enormous blind spot.
How to ask
Here is the method.
It is unglamorous and it works.
Ask in person, one at a time.
Not by group message. Not from the front. Sit down with them.
Ask for a specific role, not for help.
“We need volunteers” gets nothing. “I’d like you to run the welcome team at the second service” gets an answer.
Say why you asked them.

This is the part new leaders skip, and it is the most powerful sentence in the conversation. “I’ve watched how you talk to people who come in on their own, and I think you’d be very good at this.” People say yes to being seen.

Give them the whole picture up front: the tasks, hours, commitment length, training and reporting relationship. Explain any eligibility criteria, references, safeguarding checks or supervision required before they begin.
Set an end date.

“Would you take this for six months, and then we will both review it?” A clear review point makes the commitment easier to understand and gives both of you an honest opportunity to continue, adjust or stop.
Let them say no.

Say explicitly: “It’s completely fine to say no, and I’d rather have an honest no than a reluctant yes.” Then mean it. A leader who guilts people into serving will spend the next year managing resentment.
Give them time to answer.
“Take a week, pray about it, consider your other commitments and talk with anyone affected. Let me know next Sunday.” A considered answer is more useful than one given under pressure.
Nehemiah’s quiet lesson about ownership

Nehemiah 3 looks like a boring list of names – the record of who rebuilt which section of Jerusalem’s wall under Nehemiah’s leadership around 445 BC. But read the phrasing that repeats through it: person after person made repairs opposite his own house, or beside his own section.

Several people in Nehemiah 3 repaired sections near their homes. The chapter also names priests, tradespeople and officials taking part. Nehemiah 6:15 records the wall’s completion in fifty-two days; it does not tell us that every worker lacked construction experience.
When you are assigning, ask what part of this work the person actually cares about. People maintain what they own and abandon what they were merely given.
When they say no
Some will.
Take it graciously, and take it as information rather than rejection.

Sometimes a no concerns timing: a new baby, a hard season at work or an ill parent. Respect it. Ask whether the person would welcome a future conversation rather than assuming you should return with the same request.
Sometimes the role is simply not a fit.
Accept the first clear no. Ask again only if the person welcomes a future conversation or circumstances change and they have invited you to revisit it.
